nodes.label: Topology and Limits in the Complex Plane
nodes.explanation: Covers the complex plane as a metric space: open/closed/bounded sets, disks, domains (open connected sets), boundary and closure, connectedness and path-connectedness, convergence of complex sequences and series, and limits/continuity of complex-valued functions of a complex variable. Assumes fluency with complex arithmetic, polar/exponential form, and real single-variable calculus already; does not cover differentiability (that starts the next node) or integration.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: DISTANCE, NEIGHBORHOODS, AND OPEN SETS ===

Consider the function \( f(z) = \dfrac{(\operatorname{Re} z)(\operatorname{Im} z)}{\lvert z \rvert^2} \) for \( z \neq 0 \), and ask what happens to \( f(z) \) as \( z \) approaches \( 0 \). Along the real axis, \( \operatorname{Im} z = 0 \), so \( f(z) = 0 \) the whole way in. Along the imaginary axis, \( \operatorname{Re} z = 0 \), so again \( f(z) = 0 \). A student trained only on real-variable limits, where "approaching a point" means coming from the left or the right, might reasonably stop here and declare the limit \( 0 \). But writing \( z = r e^{i\theta} \) gives \( f(z) = \cos\theta \sin\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) \), a value that depends only on the angle of approach and not at all on how close \( z \) is to \( 0 \). Along the ray \( \theta = \pi/4 \) (the line \( y = x \)), \( f(z) = \tfrac{1}{2} \) for every point on that ray, no matter how near the origin. Two directions of approach, two different answers. In the real line there are only two directions to approach a point from; in the plane there are infinitely many, and a definition of "limit" that only checks a couple of them is not checking enough. Making this precise — what it even means for a point to be "near" another point in \( \mathbb{C} \), and what it means for a set of such points to have no gaps, no missing edges, or to come in one connected piece rather than several — is the business of this document, and it is what the definition of a limit in Section 6 will ultimately depend on.

The starting point is a notion of distance. For \( z_1, z_2 \in \mathbb{C} \), the distance between them is \( \lvert z_1 - z_2 \rvert \), the modulus of their difference. This is already familiar arithmetic, and its basic properties — \( \lvert z_1 - z_2 \rvert \geq 0 \) with equality only when \( z_1 = z_2 \), symmetry \( \lvert z_1 - z_2 \rvert = \lvert z_2 - z_1 \rvert \), and the triangle inequality \( \lvert z_1 - z_3 \rvert \leq \lvert z_1 - z_2 \rvert + \lvert z_2 - z_3 \rvert \) — are consequences of properties of the modulus already established elsewhere. What matters here is that this distance function lets every question about "closeness" in \( \mathbb{C} \) be phrased geometrically.

The basic neighborhood of a point \( z_0 \) is the open disk \( D(z_0, r) = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : \lvert z - z_0 \rvert < r \} \), the set of points strictly within distance \( r \) of \( z_0 \). It is open, not closed, by choice: the boundary circle \( \lvert z - z_0 \rvert = r \) is deliberately excluded, so that every point already inside the disk has some room around it. This is exactly what licenses the next definition. A set \( S \subseteq \mathbb{C} \) is called open if every \( z \in S \) is the center of some disk \( D(z, r) \) (with \( r \) depending on \( z \)) that is entirely contained in \( S \). The phrase "depending on \( z \)" matters: near the "middle" of a set there may be lots of room, while near a place where the set pinches close to its own edge, only a very small \( r \) will work — the definition only asks that some positive \( r \) exists for each point, not a single \( r \) that works everywhere.

A set is closed if its complement \( \mathbb{C} \setminus S \) is open. A set is bounded if it is contained in some disk \( D(0, R) \) for a finite \( R \) — equivalently, if \( \sup_{z \in S} \lvert z \rvert \) is finite. These three properties are independent of one another: a set can be open and bounded, closed and unbounded, bounded but neither open nor closed, and so on.

[TABLE]
Property | Definition | Example
Open | every point has a disk \( D(z,r) \subseteq S \) | \( D(0,1) = \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \)
Closed | complement \( \mathbb{C} \setminus S \) is open | \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert \le 1 \} \)
Bounded | \( S \subseteq D(0,R) \) for some finite \( R \) | \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 5 \} \)
[/TABLE]

The open disk itself is the cleanest example of an open set: for \( z \in D(z_0, r) \), let \( \rho = r - \lvert z - z_0 \rvert > 0 \). Any \( w \) with \( \lvert w - z \rvert < \rho \) satisfies, by the triangle inequality, \( \lvert w - z_0 \rvert \leq \lvert w - z \rvert + \lvert z - z_0 \rvert < \rho + \lvert z - z_0 \rvert = r \), so \( D(z, \rho) \subseteq D(z_0, r) \). This is the general pattern used to certify that a set is open: given an arbitrary point, exhibit a radius that works.

[QUESTION 1]
Which of the following subsets of \( \mathbb{C} \) is open but not bounded?

(A) \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert \le 3 \} \)
(B) \( \{ z : \lvert z - 2i \rvert = 1 \} \)
(C) \( \{ z : \operatorname{Re} z > -1 \} \)
(D) \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \cup \{2\} \)
(E) \( \{ z : \operatorname{Im} z \ge 0 \} \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: BOUNDARY, CLOSURE, AND INTERIOR ===

Openness is a statement about a set from the inside — every point has breathing room. It says nothing about what the set looks like from the outside, and in particular it says nothing about the points that sit right at the edge, in either direction. A point \( z_0 \) (whether or not it belongs to \( S \)) is a boundary point of \( S \) if every disk \( D(z_0, r) \), for every \( r > 0 \), contains at least one point of \( S \) and at least one point of \( \mathbb{C} \setminus S \). The collection of all such points is the boundary of \( S \), written \( \partial S \). The closure of \( S \), written \( \overline{S} \), is \( S \cup \partial S \): the set together with whatever edge it has. The interior of \( S \), written \( S^\circ \), is the set of points of \( S \) that have some disk around them entirely inside \( S \) — precisely the condition that made \( S \) open when it held at every point. A set is open exactly when \( S = S^\circ \), and closed exactly when \( S = \overline{S} \), i.e. when \( S \) already contains its own boundary.

Consider \( S = \{ z : 0 < \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \), the open unit disk with its center removed. Every point of \( S \) is an interior point: for \( z \) with \( 0 < \lvert z \rvert < 1 \), the smaller of \( \lvert z \rvert \) and \( 1 - \lvert z \rvert \) gives a workable disk radius, so \( S \) is open, matching intuition. Its boundary is more interesting than it first looks. The unit circle \( \{ \lvert z \rvert = 1 \} \) is boundary as expected — any disk around such a point catches points just inside \( S \) and points just outside with \( \lvert z \rvert > 1 \). But \( 0 \) is also a boundary point, even though it sits nowhere near that circle: any disk \( D(0, r) \), however small, contains points \( z \) with \( 0 < \lvert z \rvert < r \), which lie in \( S \), and it also contains \( 0 \) itself, which does not lie in \( S \) (since \( S \) requires \( \lvert z \rvert > 0 \) strictly). So \( 0 \) satisfies the definition of a boundary point even though it is an isolated distance from the rest of \( \partial S \) — the definition never asked for the boundary to be a single connected curve, only that every neighborhood of the point straddle \( S \) and its complement. This is why the definition is phrased in terms of every disk touching both sides, rather than in terms of some more visual notion like "edge of a region": a punctured disk has an edge that is not just its outer rim. The closure of \( S \) is \( \overline{S} = S \cup \partial S = \{ z : \lvert z \rvert \leq 1 \} \), the full closed disk, since adjoining both the missing center and the missing circle to \( S \) fills it in completely.

[QUESTION 2]
Let \( S = \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \text{ and } \operatorname{Im} z > 0 \} \), the open upper half of the unit disk. Which of the following points is an interior point of \( S \)?

(A) \( 0 \)
(B) \( i/2 \)
(C) \( 1 \)
(D) \( i \)
(E) \( -1 \)
[/QUESTION]

A domain — the term used going forward for the natural setting of a function of a complex variable — will turn out to be an open set with one further property, taken up next: it must come in a single connected piece.

=== SECTION 3: CONNECTEDNESS, PATH-CONNECTEDNESS, AND DOMAINS ===

A set \( S \) is disconnected if it can be split as \( S = A \cup B \) where \( A \) and \( B \) are nonempty, disjoint, and both open relative to \( S \) (meaning each is the intersection of an open subset of \( \mathbb{C} \) with \( S \)); such a pair is called a separation of \( S \). A set is connected if no separation exists. This definition is deliberately about the impossibility of a certain kind of split, rather than about any visual notion of "one piece," because the visual notion is exactly what needs pinning down.

A more hands-on notion is path-connectedness: \( S \) is path-connected if any two points of \( S \) can be joined by a continuous path lying entirely in \( S \). It is intuitively clear that a path-connected set cannot be separated — a path from a point of \( A \) to a point of \( B \) would have to cross from one to the other, and continuity would force it through a point belonging to neither piece cleanly, contradicting that \( A \) and \( B \) partition \( S \) — so path-connected always implies connected. The converse is not true for general sets, but it is true for open sets, and this is the fact worth proving in full, since it is what lets "connected" and "path-connected" be used interchangeably for domains from here on.

Claim: if \( S \subseteq \mathbb{C} \) is open and connected, it is path-connected, and in fact any two points of \( S \) can be joined by a polygonal path (a path made of finitely many straight segments) lying in \( S \).

Fix \( z_0 \in S \) and let \( U = \{ z \in S : \text{some polygonal path in } S \text{ joins } z_0 \text{ to } z \} \). \( U \) is nonempty, since \( z_0 \in U \) trivially (a path of zero segments). \( U \) is open: for \( w \in U \), openness of \( S \) gives a disk \( D(w, r) \subseteq S \); every point \( u \) of this disk is joined to \( w \) by the straight segment \( [w, u] \), which lies in the disk and hence in \( S \), so appending this segment to the polygonal path from \( z_0 \) to \( w \) gives a polygonal path from \( z_0 \) to \( u \); hence \( D(w,r) \subseteq U \). The complement \( S \setminus U \) is open by the same argument run in reverse: for \( w \in S \setminus U \), take a disk \( D(w,r) \subseteq S \); if any point \( u \) of this disk were in \( U \), the segment \( [u, w] \) together with a polygonal path from \( z_0 \) to \( u \) would produce one from \( z_0 \) to \( w \), putting \( w \) in \( U \), a contradiction; so \( D(w,r) \subseteq S \setminus U \). Now \( U \) and \( S \setminus U \) are disjoint open sets whose union is \( S \); if \( S \setminus U \) were nonempty, this pair would be a separation of \( S \), contradicting connectedness. So \( S \setminus U = \emptyset \), meaning \( U = S \): every point of \( S \) is reachable from \( z_0 \) by a polygonal path. Since \( z_0 \) was arbitrary among a fixed starting point, and any two such paths can be concatenated (path from \( z \) to \( z_0 \) to \( w \)), any two points of \( S \) are joined by a polygonal path.

Openness was used twice in this proof, both times to guarantee that a whole disk — not just the one point being checked — could be added to \( U \) or to its complement. Without openness the argument breaks, and it is worth seeing a case where connected genuinely does not imply path-connected. Take \( T = \{ x + i\sin(1/x) : 0 < x \leq 1 \} \cup \{ iy : -1 \leq y \leq 1 \} \): the graph of \( \sin(1/x) \) for \( x \) near \( 0 \) oscillates faster and faster, and as \( x \to 0^+ \) the graph passes arbitrarily close to every point of the segment \( \{iy : -1 \le y \le 1\} \) on the imaginary axis without ever reaching it directly. This accumulation is enough to make \( T \) connected — no separation into two open (relative to \( T \)) pieces can be found, since any piece containing part of the oscillating graph must, by the accumulation, also touch the segment, and vice versa. Yet \( T \) is not path-connected: a continuous path starting on the segment and ending on the graph would have to make infinitely many oscillations in a finite amount of path length near \( x = 0 \), which no continuous path can do. \( T \) is not open — the segment points have no disk around them lying inside \( T \) — so this does not contradict the claim just proved; it shows why the claim needed that hypothesis.

A domain is defined as an open, connected subset of \( \mathbb{C} \). By the claim above, "connected" can equivalently be read as "path-connected" whenever the set in question is open, which every domain is by definition.

[QUESTION 3]
Which of the following sets is not a domain?

(A) \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \)
(B) \( \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \cup \{ z : \lvert z - 3 \rvert < 1 \} \)
(C) \( \{ z : \operatorname{Re} z > 0 \text{ and } \operatorname{Im} z > 0 \} \)
(D) \( \{ z : 1 < \lvert z \rvert < 2 \} \)
(E) \( \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\} \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: CONVERGENCE OF COMPLEX SEQUENCES ===

A sequence \( (z_n) \) of complex numbers converges to a limit \( L \), written \( z_n \to L \), if \( \lvert z_n - L \rvert \to 0 \) as \( n \to \infty \) — that is, for every \( \varepsilon > 0 \) there is an \( N \) such that \( n > N \) implies \( \lvert z_n - L \rvert < \varepsilon \). This is the disk-based idea from Section 1 read as a statement about eventually landing, and staying, inside \( D(L, \varepsilon) \) for every \( \varepsilon \), however small.

Every complex number splits into a real and an imaginary part, and it is natural to ask whether convergence of \( (z_n) \) is really just convergence of two real sequences in disguise. It is, and the reason is a pair of inequalities relating \( \lvert w \rvert \) to \( \lvert \operatorname{Re} w \rvert \) and \( \lvert \operatorname{Im} w \rvert \) for any complex number \( w = a + bi \): since \( \lvert w \rvert = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} \), and \( a^2 \le a^2+b^2 \) while also \( a^2 + b^2 \le a^2 + 2\lvert a \rvert \lvert b \rvert + b^2 = (\lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert)^2 \), taking square roots gives
\[ \max(\lvert a \rvert, \lvert b \rvert) \leq \lvert w \rvert \leq \lvert a \rvert + \lvert b \rvert. \]
Apply this with \( w = z_n - L \), \( a = \operatorname{Re}(z_n) - \operatorname{Re}(L) \), \( b = \operatorname{Im}(z_n) - \operatorname{Im}(L) \). Suppose \( z_n \to L \): given \( \varepsilon > 0 \), take \( N \) so that \( n > N \) implies \( \lvert z_n - L \rvert < \varepsilon \); then the left inequality gives \( \lvert \operatorname{Re}(z_n) - \operatorname{Re}(L) \rvert \le \lvert z_n - L \rvert < \varepsilon \) and likewise for the imaginary part, for the same \( N \). So \( \operatorname{Re}(z_n) \to \operatorname{Re}(L) \) and \( \operatorname{Im}(z_n) \to \operatorname{Im}(L) \). Conversely, suppose both real sequences converge: given \( \varepsilon > 0 \), choose \( N_1 \) so \( n > N_1 \) implies \( \lvert \operatorname{Re}(z_n) - \operatorname{Re}(L) \rvert < \varepsilon/2 \), and \( N_2 \) so \( n > N_2 \) implies \( \lvert \operatorname{Im}(z_n) - \operatorname{Im}(L) \rvert < \varepsilon/2 \); for \( n > \max(N_1, N_2) \), the right inequality gives \( \lvert z_n - L \rvert \le \lvert \operatorname{Re}(z_n)-\operatorname{Re}(L) \rvert + \lvert \operatorname{Im}(z_n) - \operatorname{Im}(L) \rvert < \varepsilon \). So \( z_n \to L \). Both directions hold:
\[ z_n \to L \iff \operatorname{Re}(z_n) \to \operatorname{Re}(L) \text{ and } \operatorname{Im}(z_n) \to \operatorname{Im}(L). \]
This reduces every question about complex convergence to two ordinary real-sequence questions, and it is the fact this whole document leans on repeatedly from here forward.

As a worked instance, let \( z_n = \dfrac{1}{n} + i\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n^2}\right) \). The real part \( 1/n \to 0 \) and the imaginary part \( 1 - 1/n^2 \to 1 \), both by ordinary real-sequence limits, so \( z_n \to i \).

[QUESTION 4]
Consider the sequence \( z_n = \dfrac{\cos n + i \sin n}{n} + 3 - i \). Which of the following is correct?

(A) It diverges, since \( \cos n \) and \( \sin n \) do not individually converge as \( n \to \infty \).
(B) It converges to \( 4 - i \).
(C) It converges to \( 3 - i \).
(D) It converges to \( i(3-i) \).
(E) It diverges, because the values \( e^{in} \) are dense on the unit circle and so never settle down.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 5: CONVERGENCE OF COMPLEX SERIES ===

A series \( \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n \) of complex numbers converges to a sum \( S \) if its sequence of partial sums \( S_N = \sum_{n=0}^N a_n \) converges to \( S \) as a complex sequence, in the sense of Section 4. Since that sense is itself equivalent to convergence of the real and imaginary parts separately, a complex series converges precisely when the series of real parts and the series of imaginary parts of the \( a_n \) both converge as ordinary real series — again nothing new is required beyond real-variable tools already assumed, applied to two coordinates at once.

One consequence of the definition is worth isolating on its own, independent of any specific series: if \( \sum a_n \) converges to \( S \), then \( a_n \to 0 \). This is because \( a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \) for \( n \ge 1 \), and if \( S_n \to S \) and \( S_{n-1} \to S \) (the second is the same statement shifted by one index), then \( a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \to S - S = 0 \), using that the difference of two convergent complex sequences converges to the difference of their limits (itself immediate from the triangle inequality applied to \( \lvert (S_n - S_{n-1}) - (S-S) \rvert \le \lvert S_n - S \rvert + \lvert S_{n-1}-S \rvert \)). So a complex series whose terms do not tend to \( 0 \) cannot converge.

The geometric series is the standard worked example. For fixed \( z \) with \( \lvert z \rvert < 1 \), the partial sum \( S_N = \sum_{n=0}^N z^n \) satisfies \( (1-z)S_N = 1 - z^{N+1} \) (multiply \( S_N \) by \( 1-z \) and watch the interior terms cancel), so \( S_N = \dfrac{1 - z^{N+1}}{1-z} \) for \( z \ne 1 \). Since \( \lvert z \rvert < 1 \), \( \lvert z^{N+1} \rvert = \lvert z \rvert^{N+1} \to 0 \) as \( N \to \infty \), so \( z^{N+1} \to 0 \) and \( S_N \to \dfrac{1}{1-z} \). For \( \lvert z \rvert > 1 \), \( \lvert z \rvert^{N+1} \to \infty \), so the terms themselves do not tend to \( 0 \) and the series diverges by the fact above. The boundary case \( \lvert z \rvert = 1 \) is not covered by either argument: the algebraic identity for \( S_N \) still holds, but \( z^{N+1} \) neither shrinks to \( 0 \) nor grows without bound — it simply stays on the unit circle forever, and whether the series converges has to be examined separately for each such \( z \).

[QUESTION 5]
Consider the series \( \sum_{n=1}^\infty i^n \). Which statement is correct?

(A) It converges absolutely, since \( \lvert i^n \rvert = 1 \) for every \( n \), so the terms are bounded.
(B) It converges conditionally, since the sequences of real parts and imaginary parts of the partial sums are each alternating and bounded.
(C) It converges to \( 0 \), since the four values \( i, -1, -i, 1 \) sum to \( 0 \) over each block of four consecutive terms.
(D) It diverges, since the partial sums cycle repeatedly through the four values \( 1, -1, i, -i \) without settling near any one of them.
(E) It diverges, since the terms \( i^n \) do not tend to \( 0 \), which is necessary for any complex series to converge.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 6: LIMITS OF COMPLEX FUNCTIONS ===

Let \( f \) be defined on some set containing points arbitrarily close to \( z_0 \) (though not necessarily at \( z_0 \) itself). The statement \( \lim_{z \to z_0} f(z) = L \) means: for every \( \varepsilon > 0 \) there exists \( \delta > 0 \) such that \( 0 < \lvert z - z_0 \rvert < \delta \) implies \( \lvert f(z) - L \rvert < \varepsilon \). In words, \( f(z) \) can be forced into the disk \( D(L, \varepsilon) \) by keeping \( z \) inside the punctured disk \( D(z_0, \delta) \setminus \{z_0\} \). Nothing here differs symbolically from the one-variable real definition, but the content is different in a way that matters: in \( \mathbb{R} \), a punctured interval around \( x_0 \) consists of exactly two rays, and checking a limit is sometimes done by checking left and right separately. In \( \mathbb{C} \), the punctured disk \( D(z_0,\delta)\setminus\{z_0\} \) is not a union of two pieces — it is every direction at once — and the single \( \delta \) in the definition must work simultaneously for all of them. This is exactly the gap the opening example exploited: no single \( \delta \) can make \( f(z) = (\operatorname{Re} z)(\operatorname{Im} z)/\lvert z \rvert^2 \) land near one value \( L \), because for every \( \delta \), the punctured disk \( D(0,\delta) \setminus \{0\} \) contains points with \( f(z) = 0 \) (on the axes) and points with \( f(z) = 1/2 \) (on the line \( y=x \)), however small \( \delta \) is chosen — both values are always present together, no matter how far in one looks.

This gives a general tool for showing a limit fails to exist: if \( f(z) \to L \) as \( z \to z_0 \), and \( \gamma(t) \) is any path with \( \gamma(t) \to z_0 \), then \( f(\gamma(t)) \to L \) as well, since for any \( \varepsilon \) the same \( \delta \) that controls \( f \) near \( z_0 \) eventually controls \( f(\gamma(t)) \) once \( \gamma(t) \) is within \( \delta \) of \( z_0 \), which happens for \( t \) large enough because \( \gamma(t) \to z_0 \). So if two different paths into \( z_0 \) produce two different limiting values of \( f \), no limit \( L \) can exist — every path would have to agree with it, and a single \( L \) cannot equal two different numbers. This was the underlying reason the axis approach and the \( y=x \) approach, giving \( 0 \) and \( 1/2 \) respectively, were already enough to rule out any limit at \( 0 \).

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: \( f \) restricted to the ray at angle \( \theta \), as a function of \( \theta \)
xlabel: \( \theta \)
ylabel: value of \( f \) on that ray
xrange: 0, 6.283
trace: 0.5*sin(2*x) | label: \( \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) \)
[/GRAPH]

The curve above shows the value \( f \) takes along the ray at angle \( \theta \) — a constant, independent of how far out the ray is followed, but visibly different for different \( \theta \), which is the graphical form of the same fact just proved algebraically.

Limits also connect back to sequences: \( \lim_{z\to z_0} f(z) = L \) if and only if \( f(z_n) \to L \) for every sequence \( z_n \to z_0 \) with \( z_n \ne z_0 \). This is the path criterion above specialized to sequences rather than continuous paths, and it is often the most convenient form to use in practice, since Section 4 already gives full control over sequence convergence.

[QUESTION 6]
Consider \( g(z) = \dfrac{\overline{z}}{z} \) for \( z \ne 0 \). Which statement about \( \lim_{z \to 0} g(z) \) is correct?

(A) The limit is \( 1 \), since \( g(z) \to 1 \) along the real axis, and this generalizes to every direction.
(B) The limit does not exist, since \( \lvert g(z) \rvert \to 1 \) as \( z \to 0 \), so \( g(z) \) cannot approach any single finite value.
(C) The limit does not exist, since \( g(z) \) takes different constant values along different rays through the origin, and a limit requires the same value regardless of the path of approach.
(D) The limit exists and equals \( i \), obtained by approaching along the ray \( \theta = \pi/4 \).
(E) The limit is \( 0 \), since \( \overline{z} \to 0 \) and \( z \to 0 \) together as \( z \to 0 \).
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 7: CONTINUITY ===

A function \( f \) is continuous at \( z_0 \) (a point of its domain) if \( \lim_{z \to z_0} f(z) = f(z_0) \) — the limit exists, and it agrees with the value the function actually takes there. Written out, this means for every \( \varepsilon > 0 \) there is \( \delta > 0 \) such that \( \lvert z - z_0 \rvert < \delta \) implies \( \lvert f(z) - f(z_0) \rvert < \varepsilon \); the punctured disk of the limit definition becomes an ordinary disk here, since there is no longer any need to exclude \( z_0 \) itself. \( f \) is continuous on a domain if it is continuous at every point of that domain.

Sums, differences, products, and quotients (away from zeros of the denominator) of continuous functions are continuous, by the same triangle-inequality arguments used for real-valued functions, applied coordinatewise via the equivalence from Section 4. The coordinate functions themselves, \( \operatorname{Re} z \), \( \operatorname{Im} z \), \( \overline{z} \), and \( \lvert z \rvert \), are all continuous everywhere, directly from the definitions: for instance \( \lvert \operatorname{Re}(z) - \operatorname{Re}(z_0) \rvert \le \lvert z - z_0 \rvert \) means \( \delta = \varepsilon \) always works for \( \operatorname{Re} z \). Consequently every polynomial in \( z \) is continuous on all of \( \mathbb{C} \), and every rational function is continuous everywhere its denominator is nonzero.

A subtlety worth being careful with is what happens when a formula for \( f \) is only valid away from a single point, and a value is assigned there separately.

[QUESTION 7]
Define \( h(z) = \dfrac{z^2 - 1}{z - 1} \) for \( z \ne 1 \), and \( h(1) = c \) for some constant \( c \). For which value of \( c \) is \( h \) continuous at \( z = 1 \)?

(A) \( c = 2 \)
(B) \( c = 0 \)
(C) \( c = 1 \)
(D) \( c = -2 \)
(E) \( h \) cannot be made continuous at \( z=1 \) for any choice of \( c \)
[/QUESTION]

Continuity, as defined here, is a pointwise notion — it says something about \( f \) at each point of its domain individually. Together with the topological structure of Sections 1 through 3, it sets up exactly the language needed to ask, of a function on a domain, whether it behaves not just continuously but differentiably at each point — the question taken up next.

[KEY: 1C 2B 3B 4C 5E 6C 7A]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: B]
Let \( S = \{ z : \lvert z \rvert < 1 \} \cup \{ z : \lvert z - 2 \rvert < 1 \} \), two open unit disks centered at \( 0 \) and at \( 2 \), tangent to each other at the point \( z = 1 \). Which of the following is true about \( S \)?

(A) \( S \) is connected, since the two disks share the point \( z = 1 \) on their common boundary.
(B) \( S \) is not connected, since \( z=1 \) belongs to neither open disk, so there is no path in \( S \) from a point of one disk to a point of the other without leaving \( S \).
(C) \( S \) is connected, since both disks are individually connected, and a union of connected sets is always connected.
(D) \( S \) is a domain, since it is open and bounded.
(E) \( S \) is closed, since it is built from a union of two disks.
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: A]
Evaluate \( \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{i}{2}\right)^n \).

(A) \( \dfrac{4+2i}{5} \)
(B) \( \dfrac{4-2i}{5} \)
(C) \( \dfrac{2+i}{5} \)
(D) \( 1 + \dfrac{i}{2} \)
(E) The series diverges, since \( i/2 \) is not a real number and the geometric series formula only applies to real ratios.
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Complex Differentiability and the Cauchy-Riemann Equations
nodes.explanation: Defines the complex derivative via the difference quotient, contrasts it with real (multivariable) differentiability, and derives the Cauchy-Riemann equations as necessary conditions plus the sufficient condition (continuous partials satisfying CR implies holomorphic). Introduces the term 'holomorphic'/'analytic at a point' informally as 'complex differentiable on a neighborhood'. Does not yet cover power series representations, integration, or harmonic functions in depth (those are separate nodes).

nodes.label: Convergence of Complex Power Series
nodes.explanation: Extends real power series theory to the complex setting: radius of convergence, the Cauchy-Hadamard formula, behavior on and outside the circle of convergence, uniform convergence on compact subsets, and the theorem that a power series is holomorphic term-by-term inside its radius (with the derived series having the same radius). Does not yet prove that every holomorphic function equals a power series (that is Taylor's theorem, later, which needs Cauchy's integral formula too).

nodes.label: Elementary Analytic Functions: exp, log, Powers, and Trigonometric Functions
nodes.explanation: Defines the complex exponential via its power series, derives its periodicity and functional equation, then builds the complex logarithm (multi-valuedness, principal branch, branch cuts), complex powers z^a, and the complex trigonometric/hyperbolic functions and their identities. Focuses on these specific named functions and their properties/domains of single-valuedness, not on general branch-cut theory or analytic continuation (a later node).

nodes.label: Harmonic Functions and Harmonic Conjugates
nodes.explanation: Covers Laplace's equation, the fact that the real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic, construction of a harmonic conjugate on a simply connected domain, and basic examples. Does not cover the mean value property, maximum principle for harmonic functions, or the Poisson integral/Dirichlet problem, which are handled later once Cauchy's integral formula is available.

nodes.label: Contour Integrals
nodes.explanation: Defines the complex line integral of a function along a parametrized curve, covers reparametrization invariance, linearity and path additivity, the ML inequality (estimation lemma), and the fundamental theorem for contour integrals (path-independence when an antiderivative exists). Does not include Cauchy's theorem itself or any result about when the integral of a holomorphic function around a closed curve vanishes.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: DEFINING THE INTEGRAL ALONG A CURVE ===

Imagine an engineer analyzing a signal whose value at each point of a plane is a complex number \( f(z) \), and who needs to add up the effect of that signal along a curved wire — not a straight stretch of the real axis, but an arbitrary bent path in the plane, from one endpoint to another. Ordinary integration from calculus only ever sums a function over an interval \( [a,b] \) sitting on the real line. There is, so far, no meaning attached to "integrate \( f \) along this curve," because a curve is not an interval, and it is not yet clear what the analogue of \( dz \) should even be once \( z \) is allowed to move along a bend instead of along a straight line of real numbers. Something new has to be built before that sum makes sense at all.

Start with the curve itself. A smooth curve is a function \( \gamma : [a,b] \to \mathbb{C} \) that is continuously differentiable with \( \gamma'(t) \neq 0 \) for every \( t \), so that it has a well-defined, continuously turning tangent direction at every point — the same continuity and differentiability notions introduced earlier when limits and continuity in the complex plane were first laid out. A contour is a finite chain of smooth curves joined end to end, allowing corners between pieces but no jumps. This is the object \( \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \) will be built on.

Now build the integral itself. Partition \( [a,b] \) into points \( a = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b \), and let \( z_k = \gamma(t_k) \) be the corresponding points strung along the curve. Form the sum \( \sum_{k=1}^n f(z_k^*)\,(z_k - z_{k-1}) \) for some sample point \( z_k^* \) on the arc between \( z_{k-1} \) and \( z_k \) — this is the direct complex-plane analogue of a Riemann sum, replacing the real increment \( \Delta x \) with the complex step \( z_k - z_{k-1} \) actually taken along the curve. Because \( \gamma \) is differentiable, \( z_k - z_{k-1} = \gamma(t_k) - \gamma(t_{k-1}) \approx \gamma'(t_{k-1})\,(t_k - t_{k-1}) \) once the partition is fine, by the same local-linear approximation that underlies the derivative in the first place. Substituting this in turns the sum into \( \sum_k f(\gamma(t_k^*))\,\gamma'(t_k^*)\,\Delta t_k \), which is exactly a Riemann sum for the ordinary real integral \( \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t)\,dt \). Since \( f \) is continuous on the curve and \( \gamma' \) is continuous, that real integral exists, and the Riemann sums above converge to it as the partition mesh shrinks to zero. This is why the contour integral is defined exactly as

\[ \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \;:=\; \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t)\,dt. \]

Informally, this is just saying that a small step \( dz \) taken while walking along the curve is well approximated by the tangent vector \( \gamma'(t) \) scaled by the time increment \( dt \) — the same picture used when converting an arc-length or line integral from Cartesian into parametric form. The Riemann-sum argument above is what makes that informal picture exact rather than merely suggestive.

As a first worked case, take \( f(z) = \bar z \) (which is continuous but not holomorphic — nothing in the definition above required holomorphy) and let \( \gamma(t) = t(1+i) \) for \( t \in [0,1] \), the straight segment from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \). Then \( \gamma'(t) = 1+i \) and \( f(\gamma(t)) = \overline{t(1+i)} = t(1-i) \), so

\[ \int_\gamma \bar z\,dz = \int_0^1 t(1-i)(1+i)\,dt = \int_0^1 2t\,dt = 1, \]

using \( (1-i)(1+i) = 1 - i^2 = 2 \).

[QUESTION 1]
Let \( f(z) = \operatorname{Re}(z) \) and let \( \gamma(t) = t^2 + it \) for \( t \in [0,1] \), a curved path from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \). Compute \( \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \).

(A) \( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{i}{3} \)
(B) \( \frac{1}{3} + \frac{i}{2} \)
(C) \( 1 + \frac{i}{3} \)
(D) \( \frac{1}{2} + \frac{i}{3} \)
(E) \( \frac{i}{3} \)
[/QUESTION]

Once a contour integral can be computed from a chosen parametrization, a natural worry follows: the same curve can be walked using many different parametrizations, so does the value depend on which one is used?

=== SECTION 2: REPARAMETRIZATION INVARIANCE ===

Suppose \( \varphi : [c,d] \to [a,b] \) is a continuously differentiable bijection with \( \varphi'(s) \neq 0 \) for all \( s \); since \( \varphi' \) is continuous and never zero, it cannot change sign, so \( \varphi \) is strictly monotonic — either increasing throughout, with \( \varphi(c)=a,\ \varphi(d)=b \), or decreasing throughout, with \( \varphi(c)=b,\ \varphi(d)=a \). Let \( \tilde\gamma(s) = \gamma(\varphi(s)) \) be the same curve traced using the parameter \( s \). By the chain rule, \( \tilde\gamma'(s) = \gamma'(\varphi(s))\,\varphi'(s) \), so by definition

\[ \int_{\tilde\gamma} f(z)\,dz = \int_c^d f(\gamma(\varphi(s)))\,\gamma'(\varphi(s))\,\varphi'(s)\,ds. \]

This is precisely the right-hand side of the ordinary substitution rule for real integrals, with \( u = \varphi(s) \), \( du = \varphi'(s)\,ds \). If \( \varphi \) is increasing, substituting gives \( \int_a^b f(\gamma(u))\,\gamma'(u)\,du = \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \): the value is unchanged. If \( \varphi \) is decreasing, the substitution flips the limits of integration, giving \( \int_b^a f(\gamma(u))\,\gamma'(u)\,du = -\int_a^b f(\gamma(u))\,\gamma'(u)\,du = -\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \): the value flips sign. Intuitively, the total accumulated quantity along a wire should not care how fast it is traversed — only whether the direction of travel is reversed, which is exactly what the sign of \( \varphi' \) tracks.

As a check, take \( f(z) = z \) and \( \gamma(t) = t \) for \( t \in [0,1] \), so directly \( \int_\gamma z\,dz = \int_0^1 t\,dt = \tfrac12 \). Reparametrize with the increasing bijection \( \varphi(s) = s^3 \) on \( [0,1] \), giving \( \tilde\gamma(s) = s^3 \), \( \tilde\gamma'(s) = 3s^2 \), and

\[ \int_{\tilde\gamma} z\,dz = \int_0^1 s^3 \cdot 3s^2\,ds = 3\int_0^1 s^5\,ds = 3 \cdot \frac16 = \frac12, \]

matching, exactly as the invariance argument predicts.

[QUESTION 2]
Let \( f(z) = z^2 \) and let \( \gamma(t) = t(1-i) \) for \( t \in [0,1] \), a straight path from \( 0 \) to \( 1-i \). Let \( \tilde\gamma(s) = \gamma(1-s) \) for \( s \in [0,1] \) traverse the same path in the opposite direction. Compute \( \int_{\tilde\gamma} f(z)\,dz \).

(A) \( -\frac23 - \frac{2i}{3} \)
(B) \( \frac23 + \frac{2i}{3} \)
(C) \( \frac23 - \frac{2i}{3} \)
(D) \( -\frac23 + \frac{2i}{3} \)
(E) \( \frac43 + \frac{4i}{3} \)
[/QUESTION]

The value of a contour integral is therefore a property of the oriented curve, not of the particular clock used to walk along it. The next question is how such integrals behave under the two most basic algebraic operations: combining functions, and combining curves.

=== SECTION 3: LINEARITY AND PATH ADDITIVITY ===

Linearity in the integrand follows immediately from linearity of the defining real integral: for constants \( \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{C} \),

\[ \int_\gamma \big(\alpha f(z) + \beta g(z)\big)\,dz = \int_a^b \big(\alpha f(\gamma(t)) + \beta g(\gamma(t))\big)\gamma'(t)\,dt = \alpha\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz + \beta \int_\gamma g(z)\,dz, \]

since the real (Riemann) integral of a linear combination is that same linear combination of the real integrals — the identical fact used when splitting \( \int (af+bg) \) into \( a\int f + b\int g \) for real-valued functions.

Additivity over concatenated paths comes directly from how a contour was defined: if \( \Gamma \) is the contour formed by following a smooth curve \( \gamma_1 \) from \( z_0 \) to \( z_1 \) and then a smooth curve \( \gamma_2 \) from \( z_1 \) to \( z_2 \), the integral over \( \Gamma \) is defined piece by piece as \( \int_{\Gamma} f(z)\,dz = \int_{\gamma_1} f(z)\,dz + \int_{\gamma_2} f(z)\,dz \), matching how the underlying real integral over \( [a,b] \) already splits as \( \int_a^b = \int_a^{t_1} + \int_{t_1}^b \) at any interior breakpoint.

[TABLE]
Property | Statement | Where it comes from
Linearity | \( \int_\gamma (\alpha f + \beta g)\,dz = \alpha\int_\gamma f\,dz + \beta\int_\gamma g\,dz \) | Linearity of the real integral \( \int_a^b \)
Additivity | \( \int_{\gamma_1+\gamma_2} f\,dz = \int_{\gamma_1} f\,dz + \int_{\gamma_2} f\,dz \) | Splitting \( \int_a^b \) at an interior breakpoint
[/TABLE]

For a first illustration of linearity, take \( f(z) = 3z+2 \) along \( \gamma(t) = it \), \( t\in[0,1] \) (the segment from \( 0 \) to \( i \), so \( \gamma'(t)=i \)). Directly, \( f(\gamma(t)) = 3it+2 \), so \( \int_\gamma f\,dz = \int_0^1 (3it+2)(i)\,dt = \int_0^1(-3t+2i)\,dt = -\tfrac32+2i \). Splitting instead: \( \int_\gamma z\,dz = \int_0^1 (it)(i)\,dt = -\tfrac12 \), so \( 3\int_\gamma z\,dz = -\tfrac32 \); and \( \int_\gamma 2\,dz = 2(\gamma(1)-\gamma(0)) = 2i \). The sum \( -\tfrac32+2i \) matches.

For additivity, take \( f(z)=z \) along the two-segment contour \( \Gamma \) from \( 0 \) to \( 1 \) (call this \( \gamma_1(t)=t \)) and then from \( 1 \) to \( 1+i \) (call this \( \gamma_2(t)=1+it \)), each for \( t\in[0,1] \). Then \( \int_{\gamma_1} z\,dz = \int_0^1 t\,dt = \tfrac12 \), and \( \int_{\gamma_2} z\,dz = \int_0^1 (1+it)(i)\,dt = \int_0^1 (i-t)\,dt = i - \tfrac12 \). Adding gives \( \int_\Gamma z\,dz = \tfrac12 + (i-\tfrac12) = i \).

[QUESTION 3]
Let \( f(z) = 2z+1 \). Let \( \Gamma \) be the contour consisting of the segment from \( 0 \) to \( i \) followed by the segment from \( i \) to \( 1+i \). Compute \( \int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz \).

(A) \( 1 - 3i \)
(B) \( -1 + 3i \)
(C) \( 3 + i \)
(D) \( 1 + 3i \)
(E) \( 2 + 3i \)
[/QUESTION]

Linearity and additivity make contour integrals easy to manipulate algebraically, but they say nothing about the size of an integral — only how to break it apart. For many purposes, an outright bound on \( |\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz| \) is more useful than an exact value, especially when \( f \) is only known qualitatively.

=== SECTION 4: THE ML INEQUALITY (ESTIMATION LEMMA) ===

The relevant bound rests on a fact about real integrals of complex-valued functions that is easy to use without ever seeing why it is true: for continuous \( g:[a,b]\to\mathbb{C} \),

\[ \left| \int_a^b g(t)\,dt \right| \le \int_a^b |g(t)|\,dt. \]

This is not obvious the way the real-valued triangle inequality \( |\sum x_k| \le \sum |x_k| \) is, because the left side is the modulus of a single complex number while the right side is built from moduli taken one point at a time. To see why it holds, let \( w = \int_a^b g(t)\,dt \). If \( w=0 \) the inequality is trivial, so suppose \( w \ne 0 \) and write \( w = |w|e^{i\theta} \) in polar form. Then

\[ |w| = e^{-i\theta} w = e^{-i\theta}\int_a^b g(t)\,dt = \int_a^b e^{-i\theta} g(t)\,dt. \]

The left side, \( |w| \), is a real number, so the integral on the right must equal its own real part:

\[ |w| = \int_a^b \operatorname{Re}\big(e^{-i\theta}g(t)\big)\,dt \le \int_a^b \big|e^{-i\theta}g(t)\big|\,dt = \int_a^b |g(t)|\,dt, \]

using \( \operatorname{Re}(\zeta) \le |\zeta| \) for any complex \( \zeta \), and \( |e^{-i\theta}|=1 \). This proves the lemma. Informally, this is just the complex-plane version of bounding a real integral by its typical size times its width — the polar-form trick above is only what is needed to make "typical size" precise when the integrand itself is complex.

Applying this to a contour integral: with \( M = \max_{z \text{ on } \gamma} |f(z)| \) (which exists by the extreme value theorem, since \( f \) is continuous on the compact image of \( \gamma \)) and \( L = \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt \) (the arc length of \( \gamma \), the same formula used for arc length in real calculus),

\[ \left| \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \right| = \left| \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt \right| \le \int_a^b |f(\gamma(t))|\,|\gamma'(t)|\,dt \le M \int_a^b |\gamma'(t)|\,dt = ML. \]

As a worked case, let \( f(z) = e^z \) and let \( \gamma \) be the upper unit semicircle, \( \gamma(\theta) = e^{i\theta} \) for \( \theta \in [0,\pi] \), so \( L = \pi \). On this curve, \( |e^z| = |e^{\cos\theta + i\sin\theta}| = e^{\cos\theta} \), maximized at \( \theta = 0 \), giving \( M = e \). Hence \( \left|\int_\gamma e^z\,dz\right| \le e\pi \).

[GRAPH]
type: parametric2d
title: The upper unit semicircle used to bound \( \int_\gamma e^z\,dz \)
xlabel: \( \operatorname{Re}(z) \)
ylabel: \( \operatorname{Im}(z) \)
trange: 0, 3.14159
trace: cos(t), sin(t) | label: \( \gamma \)
[/GRAPH]

[QUESTION 4]
Let \( f(z) = \frac{1}{z+2} \) and let \( \gamma \) be the circle \( |z|=1 \), traversed once. Find the smallest upper bound the ML inequality provides for \( \left| \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \right| \).

(A) \( \pi \)
(B) \( 2\pi \)
(C) \( \frac{2\pi}{3} \)
(D) \( \frac{\pi}{2} \)
(E) \( 4\pi \)
[/QUESTION]

The ML inequality bounds a contour integral without computing it exactly. The last question this document settles is the opposite one: when can a contour integral be computed exactly, without any reference at all to the particular path taken?

=== SECTION 5: THE FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM FOR CONTOUR INTEGRALS ===

Suppose \( F \) is holomorphic on a domain \( D \) containing the contour \( \gamma:[a,b]\to D \), with \( F' = f \) continuous on \( D \). Define \( h(t) = F(\gamma(t)) \). Since \( F \) is differentiable at each point of the curve and \( \gamma \) is differentiable in \( t \), the chain rule gives

\[ h'(t) = F'(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t) = f(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t). \]

Writing \( h(t) = u(t) + iv(t) \) for real-valued \( u,v \), the derivative \( h'(t) \) exists and is continuous, so \( u'(t) \) and \( v'(t) \) exist and are continuous too, and the ordinary real Fundamental Theorem of Calculus applies separately to each: \( \int_a^b u'(t)\,dt = u(b)-u(a) \) and likewise for \( v \). Combining these real and imaginary parts back together,

\[ \int_a^b h'(t)\,dt = h(b) - h(a). \]

But \( \int_a^b h'(t)\,dt = \int_a^b f(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)\,dt = \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \) by the very definition from Section 1. So

\[ \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz = F(\gamma(b)) - F(\gamma(a)), \]

which depends only on the two endpoints \( \gamma(a) \) and \( \gamma(b) \), not on which path between them was used — provided the whole path stays inside the domain \( D \) where \( F \) is defined and satisfies \( F'=f \). Informally, this is the same "antiderivatives undo derivatives" idea from ordinary calculus, just carried out along a path instead of along the real line; the derivation above is only what is needed to be sure that idea survives the trip from a real interval to a curve in the plane.

As an illustration, take \( f(z)=z \), which has antiderivative \( F(z) = z^2/2 \) on all of \( \mathbb{C} \), and the same straight path from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \) used for \( \bar z \) back in Section 1. Here

\[ \int_\gamma z\,dz = F(1+i) - F(0) = \frac{(1+i)^2}{2} = \frac{2i}{2} = i, \]

and this value would come out the same along any other path from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \) — in sharp contrast to \( \bar z \), which has no antiderivative on \( \mathbb{C} \) and whose integral genuinely depended on the path chosen back in Section 1.

[QUESTION 5]
Let \( f(z) = 3z^2 - 1 \), and let \( \gamma \) be any contour from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \) lying in a domain where \( f \) has an antiderivative. Compute \( \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \).

(A) \( -3 - i \)
(B) \( -3 + i \)
(C) \( 3 + i \)
(D) \( -2 + i \)
(E) \( -1 + i \)
[/QUESTION]

[KEY: 1D 2B 3D 4B 5B]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: C]
Let \( \gamma_1 \) be any smooth curve from \( 0 \) to \( 2 \), and let \( \gamma_2(t) = \gamma_1(1-t) \) be the same curve traversed backward, from \( 2 \) back to \( 0 \). Let \( \Gamma \) be the contour formed by \( \gamma_1 \) followed by \( \gamma_2 \). For a continuous but otherwise arbitrary function \( f \), what is \( \int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz \)?

(A) equals \( 2\int_{\gamma_1} f(z)\,dz \)
(B) \( 0 \) only if \( f \) is holomorphic
(C) \( 0 \) for every continuous \( f \), always
(D) equals \( 2L \), where \( L \) is the length of \( \gamma_1 \)
(E) depends on the specific parametrization chosen for \( \gamma_1 \)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: D]
Let \( f(z) = \dfrac{1}{z^2+4} \), and let \( \gamma \) be the right half of the circle \( |z|=3 \), traversed from \( -3i \) to \( 3i \). Find the smallest upper bound the ML inequality provides for \( \left| \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \right| \).

(A) \( 3\pi \)
(B) \( \frac{\pi}{5} \)
(C) \( \frac{9\pi}{5} \)
(D) \( \frac{3\pi}{5} \)
(E) \( \frac{3\pi}{13} \)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 3]
[ANSWER: C]
Let \( f(z) = 2z + \bar z \), and let \( \gamma(t) = t + it^2 \) for \( t \in [0,1] \), a curved path from \( 0 \) to \( 1+i \). Compute \( \int_\gamma f(z)\,dz \).

(A) \( 1 + \frac{2i}{3} \)
(B) \( 2i + \frac13 \)
(C) \( 1 + \frac{7i}{3} \)
(D) \( \frac73 + i \)
(E) \( 1 - \frac{7i}{3} \)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Cauchy's Theorem (Cauchy-Goursat)
nodes.explanation: States and proves that the contour integral of a holomorphic function over a closed curve in a simply connected domain is zero, covering both the easy proof via Green's theorem (assuming continuous derivative) and Goursat's proof removing that assumption, plus the homotopy/deformation version for general domains. Needs both the integration machinery (contour_integration) and the notion of holomorphic function (complex_differentiability_cr); neither alone gives this result. Does not yet derive the integral representation formula for f(z0) (next node).

nodes.label: Cauchy's Integral Formula
nodes.explanation: Derives the formula expressing f(z0) as a contour integral of f(z)/(z-z0), and extends it (by differentiating under the integral sign) to the formula for all higher derivatives f^(n)(z0), establishing that holomorphic functions are automatically infinitely differentiable. The derivative formula is kept in this node since it is a direct extension of the same integral, not a separate technique. Does not cover Liouville's theorem, Morera's theorem, or Taylor series (separate nodes).

nodes.label: Cauchy Estimates, Liouville's Theorem, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, and Morera's Theorem
nodes.explanation: A family of direct consequences of Cauchy's integral formula: Cauchy's estimates on derivatives, Liouville's theorem (bounded entire functions are constant), the resulting proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, and Morera's theorem (the converse of Cauchy's theorem: vanishing contour integrals imply holomorphy). Grouped together because each is a short, direct application of the same formula rather than requiring new machinery; none belongs with Taylor series or singularity theory.

nodes.label: Taylor's Theorem for Holomorphic Functions
nodes.explanation: Proves that every function holomorphic on a disk equals its Taylor series there (analyticity = holomorphy), using Cauchy's integral formula to derive the coefficients and power-series convergence theory to interpret and justify the resulting expansion. Needs both threads directly: without the integral formula there is no way to produce the coefficients, and without power-series convergence theory the expansion cannot be shown to converge properly. Does not cover Laurent series (functions with singularities, expanded on an annulus) or zero sets (identity theorem, next).

nodes.label: Isolated Zeros and the Identity Theorem
nodes.explanation: Uses the local Taylor expansion to show zeros of a non-identically-zero holomorphic function are isolated, defines the order of a zero, and proves the identity theorem (two holomorphic functions agreeing on a set with a limit point in a connected domain are equal everywhere there). Does not cover the open mapping theorem, maximum modulus, or analytic continuation across a larger region (separate nodes building on this one).

nodes.label: Open Mapping Theorem, Maximum Modulus Principle, and Schwarz Lemma
nodes.explanation: Proves the open mapping theorem for non-constant holomorphic functions using the local zero-counting argument from the identity theorem, derives the maximum modulus principle and minimum modulus principle as consequences, and covers the Schwarz lemma as a key application on the unit disk. Grouped as one family since each result follows quickly from the open mapping argument; does not cover normal families or the Riemann mapping theorem (later nodes that use this one).

nodes.label: Laurent Series
nodes.explanation: Develops two-sided (positive and negative power) series expansions on an annulus, via integration over two circles and letting the inner radius shrink / outer radius grow, proving existence and uniqueness of the Laurent expansion. Distinct from Taylor's theorem because it requires the annulus-decomposition argument and negative-power terms, which are genuinely new machinery, not a restatement of the disk case. Needs both Cauchy's integral formula (for the coefficient integrals) and power-series convergence theory (for the two convergent pieces). Does not classify the type of singularity this reveals (next node).

nodes.label: Classification of Isolated Singularities
nodes.explanation: Uses the Laurent expansion to classify isolated singularities as removable, poles (with order), or essential, proves Riemann's removable singularity theorem and the Casorati-Weierstrass theorem on the behavior near essential singularities. Does not cover residues or the residue theorem itself, only the classification that residue theory is built on.

nodes.label: Residues and the Residue Theorem
nodes.explanation: Defines the residue of a function at an isolated singularity, gives computational formulas for poles of given order, and states and proves the residue theorem (a contour integral equals 2*pi*i times the sum of enclosed residues), building on the singularity classification and the earlier Cauchy theory. Does not cover the specific techniques for evaluating real integrals or the argument principle (separate application nodes).

nodes.label: Evaluating Real Integrals via Residues
nodes.explanation: Covers the standard families of contour-integration techniques for real integrals: rational functions over the real line via semicircular contours, integrals of rational functions of sine and cosine via the unit circle, Jordan's lemma for integrals with oscillatory factors, and indented contours for handling simple poles on the real axis. Purely an application node; does not introduce new general theorems beyond the residue theorem it draws on.

nodes.label: The Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem
nodes.explanation: Uses the residue theorem to derive the argument principle (a contour integral counts zeros minus poles inside a curve), and proves Rouché's theorem for comparing zero counts of two functions, with applications such as an alternate proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and locating roots. Distinct from residue_calculus_applications, which evaluates real integrals rather than counting zeros/poles; both are independent applications of the residue theorem.

nodes.label: Conformal Mappings
nodes.explanation: Defines conformality (local angle- and orientation-preservation), proves the correspondence between holomorphic functions with nonvanishing derivative and conformal maps, and works through key examples (z^2, exp(z), the Joukowski map) using the elementary functions already established. Does not cover Möbius transformations as a family in depth, or the Riemann mapping theorem (later nodes).

nodes.label: Möbius Transformations
nodes.explanation: Studies fractional linear transformations (z -> (az+b)/(cz+d)) as a specific family of conformal automorphisms of the extended complex plane: group structure under composition, fixed points, the cross-ratio, the property that circles and lines map to circles and lines, classification into elliptic/parabolic/hyperbolic/loxodromic types, and the Riemann sphere model. Assumes conformal mapping already covers the general angle-preservation framework; this node is about this one named family and its special properties.

nodes.label: Normal Families, Montel's Theorem, and Hurwitz's Theorem
nodes.explanation: Defines locally uniform convergence and equicontinuity for families of holomorphic functions, proves Montel's theorem (locally bounded implies normal) using the Cauchy estimates for equicontinuity, and proves Hurwitz's theorem (zeros of a locally-uniform limit are limits of zeros) using the identity theorem. Needs both threads directly: the boundedness-to-equicontinuity argument requires Cauchy estimates, and Hurwitz's proof requires the identity theorem's isolated-zeros structure. Sets up the compactness argument used in the Riemann mapping theorem.

nodes.label: The Riemann Mapping Theorem
nodes.explanation: States and proves that every simply connected proper open subset of the complex plane is conformally equivalent to the unit disk, via an extremal-problem existence argument (using Montel's compactness for normal families), injectivity/local behavior arguments (from the open mapping and maximum modulus theory), and Möbius transformations for normalizing and establishing uniqueness up to disk automorphism. All three prerequisites are genuinely needed for distinct steps of the proof; removing any one leaves a real gap.

nodes.label: Analytic Continuation and the Monodromy Theorem
nodes.explanation: Covers continuation of a holomorphic function along a chain of overlapping disks, uniqueness of continuation along a fixed path (via the identity theorem), the monodromy theorem for path-independence under homotopy, natural boundaries, and a brief introduction to multi-valued functions/Riemann surfaces as the object that resolves path-dependent continuation. Independent of the residue-theorem and Riemann-mapping branches; converges with them later only in specific applications such as the Gamma function.

nodes.label: The Poisson Integral Formula and the Dirichlet Problem
nodes.explanation: Derives the mean value property and maximum principle for harmonic functions from the real/imaginary parts of Cauchy's integral formula, constructs the Poisson kernel on the disk, and uses it to solve the Dirichlet problem (recovering a harmonic function on the disk from continuous boundary values). Needs both the harmonic-function framework (conjugates, Laplace's equation) and Cauchy's integral formula, from which the mean value property is directly derived.

nodes.label: Weierstrass Factorization Theorem
nodes.explanation: Covers infinite products of entire functions, convergence criteria for such products, Weierstrass elementary factors, and the construction of an entire function with a prescribed discrete zero set, relying on the identity theorem's fact that zeros of a non-trivial entire function are isolated and countable. An enrichment topic beyond the core sequence; feeds into the Gamma function's product representation.

nodes.label: The Gamma Function
nodes.explanation: Studies the Gamma function as a worked capstone example: its integral definition and analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on the plane (via the functional equation, extending the factorial beyond the original domain), its simple poles and their residues at the nonpositive integers, the reflection formula, and its Weierstrass-type infinite product representation. Genuinely needs continuation theory, residue theory, and product-factorization theory together, each supplying a different structural fact about the same function. Enrichment topic, not required for any other node.
